procedural_history.impugned_order: The plaintiffs (appellants) are challenging the decree of the District Court of Monghyr, which upheld the Subordinate Judge's dismissal of their suit.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The plaintiffs initially filed a second appeal (S.A. No. 1152 of 1946) in the High Court of Patna. During the proceedings, the court determined that the correct valuation of the suit was Rs. 9,980. The plaintiffs argued that based on this revised valuation, the appeal should have been heard by the High Court as a first appeal, ignoring the District Court's judgment. The High Court rejected this argument, following previous decisions, and the plaintiffs then approached the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The plaintiffs appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that the District Court's decree should be treated as a nullity and the High Court should have heard their appeal as a first appeal. Alternatively, they argued that even if the District Court's decree was not a nullity, they suffered prejudice because their appeal was heard by a court of inferior jurisdiction (the District Court) instead of the High Court, as per Section 11 of the Suits Valuation Act. The Supreme Court ultimately dismissed the appeal, finding that no prejudice was caused to the appellants by their appeal having been heard by the District Court.

directions: The appeal is dismissed with costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether a decree passed by a Court without jurisdiction is a nullity, and whether its invalidity can be set up at any stage, including in collateral proceedings.

facts: A suit was deliberately under-valued, causing an appeal to be filed in a District Court, which was a court of inferior jurisdiction, instead of the High Court, which would have had competence if the suit had been correctly valued.
The appellants argued that because the District Court lacked the proper pecuniary jurisdiction to hear the appeal, its resulting decree was a nullity.
law: The Court affirmed the fundamental and well-established principle that a decree passed by a court without jurisdiction is a nullity.
Such a defect in jurisdiction (whether pecuniary, territorial, or related to the subject-matter) strikes at the very authority of the court to pass any decree.
The invalidity of such a decree can be set up whenever and wherever it is sought to be enforced or relied upon, including at the stage of execution and in collateral proceedings.
This type of fundamental defect cannot be cured even by the consent of the parties.
application: The Court explained that while the general principle holds true, it is modified by Section 11 of the Suits Valuation Act in cases where the lack of jurisdiction is specifically due to the over-valuation or under-valuation of a suit.

Section 11 establishes a policy that a decree should not be treated as null and void merely on the technical ground of a valuation error. The policy of the legislature is to treat objections to pecuniary and territorial jurisdiction as technical matters.

Under Section 11, a decree from a court that lacked jurisdiction due to incorrect valuation is not automatically a nullity. An objection to it will only be entertained by an appellate court if it is raised at the earliest opportunity and has resulted in prejudice on the merits of the case.
reasoning.conclusion: The Court accepted the general principle that a decree passed by a court without jurisdiction is a nullity that can be challenged at any stage. However, it held that this principle is subject to a statutory exception under Section 11 of the Suits Valuation Act. If the jurisdictional defect is due to an incorrect valuation of the suit, the resulting decree is not to be treated as a nullity and can only be challenged under the specific conditions laid out in that section, primarily a showing of prejudice on the merits.

issue.issue_text: Whether a decree passed by an appellate court that lacked pecuniary jurisdiction due to under-valuation is a nullity, or whether it can only be set aside upon proof of prejudice on the merits under Section 11 of the Suits Valuation Act.

facts: An appeal was filed and decided by a court of inferior jurisdiction (a District Court) because the original suit had been under-valued.
If the suit had been correctly valued, the appeal would have been heard by a higher court (the High Court).
The appellant argued that because the District Court lacked the necessary pecuniary jurisdiction, its decree was a nullity (void).

Alternatively, the appellant argued that having their appeal heard by an inferior court instead of the High Court was, in itself, a "prejudice on the merits" under Section 11 of the Suits Valuation Act.
law: The general principle is that a decree passed by a court without jurisdiction (whether pecuniary, territorial, or subject-matter) is a nullity.
However, Section 11 of the Suits Valuation Act creates a specific exception for defects in pecuniary jurisdiction arising from over-valuation or under-valuation.

The policy behind Section 11 (and similar provisions like Sections 21 and 99 of the Code of Civil Procedure) is that once a case is decided on its merits, the judgment should not be reversed on purely technical grounds unless it has resulted in a failure of justice or prejudice on the merits.
application: The Court rejected the argument that the District Court's decree was a nullity. It held that the situation is governed by Section 11 of the Suits Valuation Act, which prevents such a decree from being automatically void.
The Court then considered whether the change in the appellate forum (from the High Court to the District Court) constituted "prejudice" under Section 11.
It concluded that a mere change of forum is not, by itself, the kind of prejudice contemplated by the section. The Court agreed with the reasoning of three High Court full benches on this point.

The Court reasoned that if a change of forum were automatically considered prejudice, the conditional wording of Section 11 ("unless the...under-valuation...has prejudicially affected the disposal of the case on its merits") would become meaningless, as every such decree would have to be set aside.

The Court clarified that "prejudice on the merits" must be directly attributable to the under-valuation itself. A mere error in the lower court's findings of fact is not considered prejudice caused by the under-valuation.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a decree passed by an appellate court that lacked pecuniary jurisdiction due to under-valuation is not a nullity. Such a decree can only be set aside if the party challenging it proves, under Section 11 of the Suits Valuation Act, that the under-valuation has prejudicially affected the disposal of the case on its merits. The mere fact that the appeal was heard in a lower court instead of a higher one does not, in itself, constitute such prejudice.

issue.issue_text: Whether the fact that an appeal was heard by a District Court instead of the High Court due to incorrect valuation is, in itself, a matter of prejudice.

facts: Due to an incorrect under-valuation of a suit, an appeal that should have been filed in the High Court was instead heard by a District Court.
The appellants, who were the original plaintiffs and responsible for the under-valuation, later contended that this change in the appellate forum was inherently prejudicial to them.
law: The case is governed by Section 11 of the Suits Valuation Act, which addresses defects of jurisdiction arising from incorrect valuation.

Under Section 11, a decree passed by a court without proper jurisdiction due to valuation errors cannot be set aside unless the incorrect valuation has "prejudicially affected" the disposal of the suit or appeal on its merits.
application: The Court directly addressed the appellants' argument that a "change in the forum of appeal is by itself a matter of prejudice."

It rejected this argument, stating that the "prejudice contemplated by the section is something different from the fact of the appeal having been heard in a forum which would not have been competent to hear it on a correct valuation."

The Court clarified that the appellants were not deprived of their substantive right to appeal; they did have an appeal, which was heard by the District Court. The error only changed the venue of that appeal.

The Court also noted that the under-valuation had, in a way, enlarged the appellants' right of appeal, as it gave them an appeal to the District Court and then a potential second appeal to the High Court, whereas a correct valuation would have allowed only one appeal directly to the High Court.

The Court explicitly endorsed the view of three High Court Full Benches which had previously concluded that a mere change of forum is not considered prejudice within the meaning of Section 11 of the Suits Valuation Act.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the mere fact that an appeal was heard by a District Court instead of the High Court due to incorrect valuation is not, in itself, a matter of prejudice. The Court held that prejudice under Section 11 of the Suits Valuation Act must be demonstrated on the merits of the case, and a simple change in the appellate forum does not meet this requirement.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a decree passed by a Court without jurisdiction is a nullity, and whether its invalidity can be set up at any stage, including in collateral proceedings.
appellant_arguments: The decree passed in appeal by the District Court of Monghyr should be regarded as a nullity because the court lacked pecuniary jurisdiction.
respondent_arguments: The decree cannot be regarded as a nullity.
The objection to jurisdiction is highly technical and should not be entertained, especially since it was raised for the first time in the appellate court.
The appellants are attempting to take advantage of their own wrong (the under-valuation) to obstruct the plaintiff.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a decree passed by an appellate court that lacked pecuniary jurisdiction due to under-valuation is a nullity, or whether it can only be set aside upon proof of prejudice on the merits under Section 11 of the Suits Valuation Act.
appellant_arguments: The decree is a nullity due to the court's lack of pecuniary jurisdiction.
respondent_arguments: The matter is governed by Section 11 of the Suits Valuation Act, which requires proof that the under-valuation has prejudicially affected the disposal of the appeal on its merits.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the fact that an appeal was heard by a District Court instead of the High Court due to incorrect valuation is, in itself, a matter of prejudice.
appellant_arguments: Prejudice was caused because the under-valuation resulted in their appeal being heard by a court of inferior jurisdiction (the District Court) when it should have been heard by the High Court.
They were deprived of a right to two appeals, one to the District Court and another to the High Court.
respondent_arguments: The mere fact of an appeal being heard by a lower court is not, in itself, a matter of prejudice under Section 11 of the Suits Valuation Act.
No actual prejudice occurred, as there was a fair and full hearing of the appeal on the merits, and no injustice resulted from the disposal of the matter.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A judgment rendered by a court after a trial on the merits should not be reversed by an appellate court on purely technical grounds, such as an objection to territorial or pecuniary jurisdiction, unless it has resulted in a failure of justice. Such an objection is not open to consideration by an appellate court unless there has been prejudice on the merits, which must be directly attributable to the jurisdictional error (such as over-valuation or under-valuation) and is not established by a mere change of forum or an error in the decision itself. Whether prejudice has occurred is a matter to be determined on the facts of each case.
obiter: The jurisdiction to interfere on grounds of prejudice is in the nature of a revisional jurisdiction to be exercised with caution and for the ends of justice.
A party cannot be allowed to take advantage of their own wrong, such as contributing to a mistake and then seeking to benefit from it.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The policy of the Legislature is that when a case has been tried by a court on the merits and judgment rendered, it should not be liable to be reversed purely on technical grounds, such as objections to pecuniary jurisdiction, unless it has resulted in a failure of justice. A decree passed by an appellate court that lacked pecuniary jurisdiction due to under-valuation is not a nullity. Under Section 11 of the Suits Valuation Act, such a decree can only be interfered with if the under-valuation has prejudicially affected the disposal of the appeal on its merits, and the mere fact that the appeal was heard in a different or lower forum does not, in itself, constitute such prejudice.
legal_tests_applied: Under Section 11 of the Suits Valuation Act, an objection to jurisdiction based on over-valuation or under-valuation will not be entertained by an appellate court unless the valuation has 'prejudicially affected the disposal of the suit or appeal on its merits'.
The prejudice envisaged by Section 11 must be something other than the appeal being heard in a different forum.
Whether there has been prejudice or not is a matter to be determined on the facts of each case.
why_appellant_lost: The contention that the decree and judgment of the District Court should be treated as a nullity cannot be sustained under Section 11 of the Suits Valuation Act.

The argument that deprivation of the right to appeal to the High Court on facts must, without more, constitute prejudice was rejected. If the fact of an appeal being heard by a lower court is itself a matter of prejudice, then the words 'unless the over-valuation or under-valuation thereof has prejudicially affected the disposal of the suit or appeal on its merits' would become wholly useless.
The appellants are attempting to take advantage of their own wrong, as they contributed to the mistake of under-valuation.
The plea regarding jurisdiction is highly technical in character and was raised for the first time in the appellate court.
why_respondent_won: The matter is governed by Section 11 of the Suits Valuation Act, which requires proof that the under-valuation has prejudicially affected the disposal of the appeal on its merits.
The prejudice contemplated by the section is something different from the fact of the appeal having been heard in a forum which would not have been competent to hear it on a correct valuation.
Decrees passed in such cases are liable to be interfered with in an appellate Court, not in all cases and as a matter of course, but only if prejudice such as is mentioned in the section results.
policy_considerations: The policy underlying section 11 of the Suits Valuation Act, as also of sections 21 and 99 of the Code of Civil Procedure, is that when a case has been tried by a Court on the merits and judgment rendered, it should not be liable to be reversed purely on technical grounds, unless a failure of Justice has resulted.

The policy of the Legislature has been to treat objections as to jurisdiction, both territorial and pecuniary, as technical and not open to consideration by an appellate Court, unless there has been prejudice on the merits.
